records.statement: The figure is a multi-panel X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern showing intensity versus 2θ angle for six different samples.
The legend indicates that the cloverleaf symbol (♣) corresponds to BN and the diamond symbol (♦) corresponds to Cu.
The sample labels are BN-NS, Cu/BN-NS, BN-NF, Cu/BN-NF, BN-NP, and Cu/BN-NP, arranged from top to bottom.
The XRD patterns for BN-NF and Cu/BN-NF are magnified by 5 times, as indicated by text annotations next to the blue and teal curves.
The main BN peak is located at approximately 26-27° 2θ for all samples.
The Cu/BN-NS, Cu/BN-NF, and Cu/BN-NP samples show additional peaks around 43-45° and 50-55° 2θ, which are assigned to Cu based on the legend.
The intensity of the main BN peak is highest in the BN-NP sample and lowest in the BN-NF and Cu/BN-NF samples (after magnification).
The XRD patterns show distinct diffraction peaks corresponding to BN and Cu phases in the catalysts.
The BN-NS, BN-NF, and BN-NP samples exhibit characteristic BN diffraction peaks, with the most intense peak around 26° 2θ.
Cu/BN-NS, Cu/BN-NF, and Cu/BN-NP samples show additional diffraction peaks attributed to Cu, located around 43°, 50°, and 74° 2θ.
The XRD patterns for BN-NF and Cu/BN-NF are magnified by 5 times for better visualization of low-intensity peaks.
The intensity of the BN peak at ~26° 2θ is highest in the BN-NP sample, suggesting a higher crystallinity or preferred orientation.
The Cu diffraction peaks are more pronounced in Cu/BN-NS compared to Cu/BN-NF and Cu/BN-NP, indicating higher Cu loading or better crystallinity in the NS sample.
The BN-NF and Cu/BN-NF samples exhibit broader and less intense peaks compared to other BN supports, which may indicate lower crystallinity or smaller crystallite size.
Panel A is a line graph showing adsorption isotherms for six different materials, with adsorbed volume (V_a) on the y-axis and relative pressure (P/P₀) on the x-axis.
Panel B is a line graph showing pore size distributions (dV_p/dr_p) for the same six materials, with pore size on the x-axis and differential pore volume on the y-axis.

The adsorption-desorption isotherms for all BN supports and Cu/BN catalysts show a Type II behavior with a hysteresis loop at high relative pressure (P/P₀ > 0.8), indicating the presence of mesopores.
BN-NS exhibits the highest adsorption volume (Vₐ) among all samples, followed by BN-NF and BN-NP, suggesting a higher surface area for BN-NS.

The Cu/BN catalysts (Cu/BN-NS, Cu/BN-NF, Cu/BN-NP) show lower adsorption volumes compared to their corresponding BN supports (BN-NS, BN-NF, BN-NP), indicating a reduction in surface area or pore volume upon Cu loading.
BN-NS has a broad pore size distribution centered around 10–100 nm, while BN-NF and BN-NP show narrower distributions with peaks at smaller pore sizes (<10 nm).
The pore size distributions of Cu/BN catalysts are shifted to smaller pore sizes compared to their corresponding BN supports, indicating pore blockage or narrowing due to Cu deposition.
The Cu/BN-NP sample exhibits the smallest pore size distribution peak, suggesting the most significant pore blockage among the catalysts.
The BN-NS support has the largest pore volume, as indicated by the highest dVₚ/drₚ value in the pore size distribution plot.
The pore size distribution of BN-NF is bimodal, with peaks at approximately 2–5 nm and 10–20 nm.
The hysteresis loop in the isotherms is consistent with capillary condensation in mesopores, which is typical for materials with pore sizes between 2 and 50 nm.
The Cu/BN-NF catalyst shows a pore size distribution peak at a smaller pore size than BN-NF, suggesting that Cu nanoparticles are deposited within the pores, reducing their effective diameter.

Panels (b), (e), and (h) are red elemental maps corresponding to the SEM images in (a), (d), and (g) respectively.
Panels (c), (f), and (i) are green elemental maps corresponding to the SEM images in (a), (d), and (g) respectively.
Each panel contains a scale bar indicating the magnification.

The elemental maps (c), (f), (i) are labeled 'Pd K' in the bottom right corner.
The figure type is a composite of scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images and corresponding energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) elemental maps.
BN-NS exhibits a fibrous or nanosheet-like morphology with a tangled network structure.
BN-NF has a tubular or nanofiber morphology with a smooth surface and defined cylindrical shape.
BN-NP consists of plate-like or nanoplatelet structures with irregular, overlapping shapes.
The elemental mapping for BN-NS shows uniform distribution of B (red) and N (green) across the fibrous structure.
The elemental mapping for BN-NF shows uniform distribution of B (red) and N (green) across the nanofiber.
The elemental mapping for BN-NP shows uniform distribution of B (red) and N (green) across the nanoplatelets.
The TEM images (A, D, G) correspond to BN-NS, BN-NF, and BN-NP, respectively.
The elemental distribution maps (B, C) correspond to B and N in BN-NS.
The elemental distribution maps (E, F) correspond to B and N in BN-NF.
The elemental distribution maps (H, I) correspond to B and N in BN-NP.
The red color in maps (B, E, H) represents the distribution of boron (B).
The green color in maps (C, F, I) represents the distribution of nitrogen (N).
All three BN nanostructures (NS, NF, NP) are composed of boron and nitrogen, as confirmed by elemental mapping.
The scale bars in the images indicate different magnifications: 1.0 µm for BN-NS, 250 nm for BN-NF, and 0.5 µm for BN-NP.

TEM images show Cu nanoparticles dispersed on BN supports with different morphologies: nanosheets (NS), nanofibers (NF), and nanoparticles (NP).
In Cu/BN-NS, Cu nanoparticles appear as bright, discrete spots distributed over a lamellar BN nanosheet structure.
In Cu/BN-NF, Cu nanoparticles are dispersed on a fibrous BN support, with a more uniform distribution compared to NS.
In Cu/BN-NP, Cu nanoparticles are located on a particulate BN support, with some aggregation visible.
Elemental mapping confirms the presence of B, N, and Cu in all three Cu/BN composites.
The B and N elements are uniformly distributed across the entire BN support in all three composites, as shown by the red and green maps.
The Cu elemental distribution (yellow maps) correlates spatially with the bright spots in the TEM images, confirming the location of Cu nanoparticles.
The Cu nanoparticles in Cu/BN-NS are more uniformly distributed compared to Cu/BN-NP, where some clustering is observed.
The scale bars indicate that the images cover different magnifications: 100 nm for NS and NP, and 0.5 µm for NF.
The elemental maps for B, N, and Cu are presented for each composite, with B in red, N in green, and Cu in yellow.

records.statement: The B 1s XPS spectrum of BN-NS shows a dominant peak at approximately 190 eV, assigned to B-N bonding.
In the B 1s spectrum, the Cu/BN-NS sample exhibits a single, sharp peak at ~190 eV, similar to BN-NS, indicating minimal disruption of the B-N bonding upon Cu loading.
The N 1s XPS spectrum of BN-NS displays a main peak at ~398 eV, attributed to B-N bonding, with a smaller shoulder at higher binding energy assigned to B-O-N.
The N 1s spectrum of Cu/BN-NS shows a broadened peak with a shift to higher binding energy compared to BN-NS, suggesting interaction between Cu and the nitrogen sites.
The Cu 2p XPS spectrum of Cu/BN-NS reveals a distinct peak at ~935 eV, characteristic of metallic Cu, indicating the presence of Cu nanoparticles on the BN-NS support.
The Cu 2p spectrum of Cu/BN-NF shows a very weak signal, suggesting a low Cu loading or poor dispersion on the BN-NF support.
The Cu 2p spectrum of Cu/BN-NP displays a strong peak at ~935 eV, indicating a high Cu loading or well-defined Cu nanoparticles on the BN-NP support.
The B 1s spectra of BN-NF and Cu/BN-NF show a broad peak with multiple components, suggesting a more disordered or defective structure compared to BN-NS.
The N 1s spectra of BN-NF and Cu/BN-NF exhibit a broad peak with a significant contribution from B-O-N, indicating a higher oxygen content or surface oxidation compared to BN-NS.
The B 1s spectrum of BN-NP shows a sharp peak at ~190 eV, similar to BN-NS, suggesting a well-defined crystalline structure.
The N 1s spectrum of BN-NP is similar to BN-NS, with a dominant B-N peak and a small B-O-N shoulder, indicating a low defect density and minimal surface oxidation.

The Cu 2p spectra of Cu/BN-NS and Cu/BN-NP show a clear metallic Cu peak, while Cu/BN-NF shows a very weak signal, indicating that Cu loading and/or dispersion are highly dependent on the BN support morphology.

The binding energy of the B-N peak in the B 1s spectrum is approximately 190 eV for all BN-based samples, indicating a consistent chemical environment for boron in the B-N bond across different morphologies.
The binding energy of the N 1s peak assigned to B-N is approximately 398 eV for all samples, confirming the presence of the B-N bond in all BN materials.
The presence of a B-O-N component in the N 1s spectra suggests surface oxidation or the presence of oxygen-containing functional groups on the BN materials.
The figure is a UV-Vis absorption spectrum showing absorbance versus wavelength for six different materials.
There are six distinct curves in the graph, each corresponding to a different material as indicated in the legend.
The x-axis is labeled 'Wavelength(nm)' and ranges from 200 to 800 nm with major tick marks every 100 nm.
The y-axis is labeled 'Absorbance(a.u.)' and has no numerical tick marks, but the scale appears to range from 0 to approximately 1.2 based on peak heights.
The curve for Cu/BN-NF (teal) exhibits the highest absorbance peak in the visible range, centered around 570 nm.
The curve for Cu/BN-NS (orange) shows a broad absorbance peak centered around 550 nm.
The curves for BN-NS (black) and BN-NF (blue) show a sharp absorption edge around 250-270 nm, with absorbance dropping rapidly beyond 300 nm.
The curves for BN-NP (pink) and Cu/BN-NP (orange) show very low absorbance across the entire visible range (400-800 nm), indicating minimal light absorption.
The UV-vis spectrum of BN-NF shows a sharp absorption peak around 250 nm and a broad absorption tail extending to 800 nm.
The Cu/BN-NF sample exhibits a broad absorption band centered around 570 nm, which is absent in the BN-NF support.
The BN-NS sample shows a sharp absorption edge near 250 nm with minimal absorption beyond 300 nm.
The Cu/BN-NS sample displays a broad absorption feature starting around 300 nm and extending to 800 nm, indicating a change in optical properties compared to BN-NS.
The BN-NP sample has a very low absorbance across the entire 200–800 nm range, suggesting a highly transparent or low-density material.
The Cu/BN-NP sample shows a slight increase in absorbance compared to BN-NP, particularly in the 300–700 nm range, indicating the presence of copper species.
The introduction of copper onto BN supports (Cu/BN) generally leads to increased optical absorption in the visible range (400–800 nm) compared to the corresponding bare BN supports.
The BN-NF support exhibits the highest absorbance in the UV region (200–300 nm) among all BN supports.
The Cu/BN-NF sample has the most pronounced visible absorption band among all samples, centered at approximately 570 nm.
The UV-vis spectra suggest that copper loading modifies the electronic structure of BN supports, leading to new absorption features in the visible region.
The figure is a line graph showing propane conversion (%) as a function of temperature (°C) for six different catalysts under thermal and photothermal conditions.
The propane conversion increases with temperature for all Cu/BN catalysts in both thermal and photothermal systems.
At 500°C, the Cu/BN-NS catalyst exhibits the highest propane conversion under photothermal conditions (approximately 4.1%) compared to other catalysts.
The photothermal system consistently achieves higher propane conversion than the thermal system for all three Cu/BN catalysts (NS, NF, NP) across the tested temperature range.
The Cu/BN-NP catalyst shows the lowest propane conversion among the three catalysts under both thermal and photothermal conditions at all temperatures.
The reaction conditions include a propane to oxygen ratio of 2:1, a total flow rate of 20.0 mL min⁻¹, and a pre-reduction of the catalyst at 500°C for 2 hours.
The photothermal system uses a 300 W Xe lamp with a cutoff wavelength of λ > 420 nm to provide irradiation.
The Cu/BN-NS catalyst has a higher propane conversion than the Cu/BN-NF catalyst under both thermal and photothermal conditions at 500°C.
The Cu/BN-NF catalyst shows a higher propane conversion than the Cu/BN-NP catalyst under both thermal and photothermal conditions at all tested temperatures.
The photothermal enhancement effect is most pronounced for the Cu/BN-NS catalyst, as indicated by the largest gap between its thermal and photothermal curves.
The propane conversion for all catalysts is below 4.5% at 500°C, indicating relatively low activity under the tested conditions.
The figure is a line graph showing product selectivity (%) as a function of temperature (°C) for various products under thermal and photothermal conditions.

markers: Solid inverted triangles for CH₄ thermal
Open inverted triangles for CH₄ photothermal

records.statement: In the thermal catalytic system, propylene selectivity decreases from approximately 80% at 400°C to around 65% at 500°C.
In the photothermal catalytic system, propylene selectivity remains relatively stable, around 75-80%, across the temperature range of 400–500°C.
CO selectivity increases with temperature in both thermal and photothermal systems, reaching approximately 15% at 500°C in the photothermal system and around 10% in the thermal system.
CO2 selectivity increases significantly with temperature in the photothermal system, rising from about 5% at 400°C to over 40% at 500°C, while in the thermal system it remains below 10%.
Ethylene selectivity decreases with increasing temperature in both systems, dropping from around 5% at 400°C to less than 2% at 500°C.
CH4 selectivity remains very low and relatively constant (below 5%) across the temperature range in both thermal and photothermal systems.
The photothermal system exhibits higher CO2 selectivity and lower propylene selectivity compared to the thermal system at higher temperatures (e.g., 500°C).
The catalyst used is Cu/BN-NS, and the reaction is propane oxidation to propylene (ODHP).
The reaction conditions include a catalyst mass of 0.10 g, pre-reduction at 500°C for 2 hours, a propane:oxygen ratio of 2:1, a total flow rate of 20.0 mL/min, and a temperature range of 400–500°C.
The photothermal system uses a 300 W Xe lamp with a cutoff wavelength of λ > 420 nm.
The photothermal system enhances CO2 selectivity at the expense of propylene selectivity compared to the thermal system, especially at higher temperatures.
The figure is a line graph showing conversion and selectivity over time on stream for a catalytic reaction.
The propane conversion remains relatively stable at approximately 4% over 8 hours of reaction time.
Propylene selectivity is consistently high, ranging from 65% to 67%, throughout the 8-hour test.
CO selectivity remains stable around 14-15% over the 8-hour period.
CO2 selectivity shows a slight decrease from ~14% to ~12% over 8 hours.
Methane and ethane selectivities remain very low and stable, below 3%, throughout the test.
The catalyst Cu/BN-NS demonstrates good stability in the photothermal catalytic ODHP system over 8 hours.
The reaction was conducted at 500°C with a 300 W Xe lamp irradiation (λ > 420 nm).
The catalyst was pre-reduced at 500°C for 2 hours before the reaction.
The gas feed ratio was propane to oxygen at 2:1 with a total flow rate of 20.0 mL min⁻¹.
